The force-matching task asks someone to reproduce a force applied to their own
finger, once by pressing directly and once by turning a dial that applies it
for them. People reproduce it accurately through the dial and overshoot when
they press themselves. The size of that overshoot is the measure, and it is
what the [schizophrenia thesis](../research/schizophrenia.qmd) uses to ask
whether self-generated sensation is attenuated the way it should be.

Doing that needs two force channels sampled together: the one applied to the
finger and the one the participant produces. The rig has both. It was designed
and machined in-house with my brother Anıl Bekdemir, a mechanical engineer,
and the acquisition software is mine.

It was built rather than bought for two reasons that turned out to be the same
reason. Commercial equivalents cost more than the whole grant, and the ones
within reach could not be changed once delivered. A task that is still being
designed needs an instrument that can still be changed.

Mechanically the rig is finished. Calibration is running now: the transducers
have to be traced against known loads across the range the task actually uses,
and that curve has to hold from one session to the next. The calibration data
and the build notes will be published together with it, since a device nobody
can rebuild is not much better than no device.
